lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, Every place on Earth has its own amazing story. Today, we follow the Sun Compass across the sea. Our little boat sails into Harbor Town on the Island of Fire. Fishing boats float in the harbor, and seagulls fly over the roofs. Behind the town stands a tall, green mountain. A little white steam rises from the top. Kiko asks, What is that mountain? A little red salamander in a yellow helmet waves from the pier. Welcome! I'm Ember, the island's junior safety ranger. That's Mount Cinder. That mountain is a volcano. Say it with me. That mountain is a volcano. Great! Riko looks a little worried. A volcano? Is it safe? Ember smiles. Don't worry. Mount Cinder is calm today, and scientists watch it every day. Then he gives us a lantern with six dark windows. This is the Safety Lantern. When you learn how to stay safe, a window will light up. Safety first, fun always! Let's read the sign at the harbor. "Welcome to the Island of Fire! Mount Cinder is a volcano. Its last eruption was about 300 years ago. Today, only a little white steam comes out of the top. Scientists at the Volcano Watch Center check the mountain day and night. Thanks to the volcano, our island has hot springs, rich soil, and beautiful views. Please enjoy your stay, and learn with us how to be safe and ready!" When was the last eruption? About 300 years ago. Who watches the mountain? Scientists at the Volcano Watch Center. Now, phonics. Rupt means break or burst. E means out. E plus rupt is erupt. To erupt means to burst out. Eruption is the noun. The last eruption was a long time ago. Erupted is the past. Mount Cinder erupted about 300 years ago, and now it's resting quietly. Next time, we will visit the Earth Science Museum and meet a volcano scientist!

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, That mountain is a volcano. Today, Ember takes us to the Earth Science Museum. In the main hall, there is a giant model of the earth. One part is cut open, like a slice of cake. A kind woman in a white coat walks over. Hello! I'm Dr. Mori. I'm a volcano scientist. I work here and at the Volcano Watch Center. She points to the colorful stripes inside the model. The earth isn't the same all the way through. The earth is made of layers. Say it with me. The earth is made of layers. Great! Haru shouts, Wow! What's in the middle? Then he covers his mouth. Oops, sorry for interrupting! Dr. Mori laughs. That's OK. Good questions are always welcome! Let's read the museum panel. "The Layers of the Earth. The earth is made of four layers. The outside layer is the crust. We live on the crust. It is very thin, like the skin of an apple. Under the crust is the mantle. It is very hot and very thick. Next comes the outer core. The inner core is in the very center. It is about as hot as the surface of the sun!" Which layer do we live on? The crust. How hot is the inner core? About as hot as the surface of the sun. Ember says, I love hot water, but that's too hot even for me! Now, phonics. Rupt means break. Inter means between. Inter plus rupt is interrupt. When you interrupt, you break into someone's talk. Interruption is the noun. Sorry for the interruption. Please go on. Interrupted is the past. Haru interrupted Dr. Mori, but he said sorry right away. How polite! Next time, we will make a model volcano erupt in the museum's science room!

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, The earth is made of layers. Today, Dr. Mori takes us to the museum's science room. On the table, there is a small clay mountain with a hole on top. Dr. Mori explains. Deep under a volcano, there is magma. Magma is melted rock under the ground. When magma comes out of a volcano, we call it lava. When a volcano erupts, hot lava comes out. Say it with me. When a volcano erupts, hot lava comes out. Great! Volcanoes can also send out ash, rocks, and gas. Riko asks, Will Mount Cinder erupt today? Dr. Mori smiles. Cameras and sensors watch Mount Cinder day and night, and today it is calm. Now, let's make our own volcano! Let's read the experiment card. "Make a Model Volcano. You need a clay volcano, a small cup, baking soda, vinegar, and red food coloring. First, put the cup inside the top of the volcano. Next, put two spoons of baking soda into the cup. Then, add a few drops of red coloring. Finally, pour in the vinegar slowly and step back. Watch the red foam bubble up and flow down the sides, just like lava!" What do you put into the cup? Two spoons of baking soda and a few drops of red coloring. What do you pour in last? The vinegar. Kiko pours the vinegar. Fizz! Whoosh! Red foam bubbles over the top. Ember claps. It's erupting! Keep your safety glasses on, everyone! Now, phonics. Erupting means bursting out right now. Look, our volcano is erupting! Rupt means break. Dis means apart. Dis plus rupt is disrupt. To disrupt means to break up the usual way things go. Disruption is the noun. Our model eruption caused a small disruption. The table got very messy! Next time, we will relax in the island hot springs with Ember!

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, When a volcano erupts, hot lava comes out. Today, Ember takes us to his favorite place, the island hot springs. Warm steam rises from a big stone pool. We sit down and put our feet in the water. Ahh! Kiko asks, Why is the water hot? Ember says, It's heated deep underground. Volcanoes aren't only about lava. They give us presents, too! Volcanoes make hot springs and new islands. Say it with me. Volcanoes make hot springs and new islands. Great! Haru looks surprised. New islands? Ember nods. Yes! The islands of Hawaii were made by volcanoes. Let's read the board next to the hot springs. "Gifts from Our Volcano. Mount Cinder gives the island many gifts. Water is heated deep underground, so we can enjoy warm hot springs. Long ago, ash from the volcano fell on the land. Old ash makes the soil rich, so farmers grow sweet potatoes and many other vegetables here. Heat from deep underground can also make electricity. This is called geothermal energy. Volcanoes even make new islands, like the islands of Hawaii." Why is the soil rich? Because of old ash from the volcano. What is geothermal energy? Energy that comes from the heat underground. Suddenly, Ember jumps up. Oh! My tail is getting too warm! He gets out of the water very quickly, and everyone laughs. Now, phonics. Rupt means break. Ab means away. Ab plus rupt is abrupt. Abrupt means very sudden. Ember made an abrupt jump. Abruptly means suddenly. Ember got out of the water abruptly! Rupture means a break or a burst, like a rupture in a water pipe. Next time, we will share everything we learned at the Earth Science Show!

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, Volcanoes make hot springs and new islands. Today is the Earth Science Show at the museum! Dr. Mori, Ember, and many island children sit in the audience. Kiko talks about the layers of the earth. Haru explains magma and lava with our model volcano. Then it's Riko's turn. She holds up a big map of the world. The crust is broken into huge pieces called plates. They are always moving, but very, very slowly. The earth's crust moves slowly. Say it with me. The earth's crust moves slowly. Great! Let's read Riko's poster. "The Moving Plates. The earth's crust is broken into huge pieces called plates. Plates move only a few centimeters a year. That is about as fast as your fingernails grow! Japan is where four plates meet, so Japan has many earthquakes and volcanoes. In fact, Japan has about 111 active volcanoes. Mount Cinder is one of them, and scientists on our island watch it every day." How fast do plates move? About as fast as your fingernails grow. How many plates meet in Japan? Four. Everyone claps. Then Ember holds up the Safety Lantern. Look! One of the six windows is glowing with a warm orange light. You learned how the earth works. That's the first step to staying safe! Now, phonics. Let's review rupt, which means break. Erupt. E means out, so a volcano bursts out. Interrupt. Inter means between, so you break into someone's talk. Nobody interrupted Riko today! Disruption. Dis means apart, so the usual way things go is broken up. Abrupt. Ab means away, and abrupt means very sudden. Next time, we will visit the earthquake corner and learn why the ground shakes!

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, The earth's crust moves slowly. Today, Dr. Mori meets us at the entrance of the earthquake corner. On a table, there are two wooden blocks with a thin sponge between them. Push them together, Dr. Mori says. Haru pushes slowly. At first, the blocks don't move. Then, snap! They slip suddenly, and the table shakes a little. That's how an earthquake works, Dr. Mori explains. Plates push against each other for a long time. Then the rocks under the ground break and move suddenly, and the ground shakes. An earthquake happens when the ground moves. Say it with me. An earthquake happens when the ground moves. Great! Let's read the panel. "Why Do Earthquakes Happen? Deep under the ground, huge plates push against each other. Little by little, the push gets stronger. One day, the rocks break and move suddenly. Then the ground shakes. This is an earthquake. Japan has many earthquakes, so it is important to be ready. During the shaking, protect your head. Stay away from windows and tall shelves, because things might fall. At home, attach tall furniture to the wall." Why does the ground shake? Because rocks under the ground break and move suddenly. What should you attach to the wall? Tall furniture. Ember says, When we are ready, we can feel safe and strong. That's the importance of learning! Now, phonics. Let's make nouns with a, n, c, e. Distant, distance. Keep a safe distance from windows. Enter, entrance. The e in e, r disappears. Important, importance. Guide, guidance. Take away the e. Thank you for your guidance, Dr. Mori! Next time, we will visit the Volcano Watch Center and learn about typhoons and heavy rain!

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, An earthquake happens when the ground moves. Today, Dr. Mori shows us the Volcano Watch Center. It's very quiet inside. In the silence, we can hear the computers humming. Many screens show Mount Cinder from different cameras. The mountain is calm, as usual. On one big screen, there is a white swirl of clouds far out at sea. Dr. Mori points to it. This is a typhoon. It's very far away, but we watch the weather every day, too. A typhoon brings strong wind and heavy rain. Say it with me. A typhoon brings strong wind and heavy rain. Great! Let's read the weather card next to the screen. "All About Typhoons. Typhoons form over warm ocean water. They come mostly in summer and fall. A typhoon brings strong wind and heavy rain. The center of a typhoon is called the eye. It is calm there, but the storm comes back soon. Heavy rain can cause floods and landslides. During a typhoon, stay inside and keep away from windows. In heavy rain, never go near rivers or the sea." Where do typhoons form? Over warm ocean water. Where should you be during a typhoon? Inside, away from the windows. Ember says, I love water, but I never go near the river in heavy rain! Dr. Mori smiles. When you know what to do, you can face a typhoon with confidence. Now, phonics. Let's change e, n, t to e, n, c, e. Silent, silence. Different, difference. What's the difference between the eye and the rest of the typhoon? The eye is calm. Confident, confidence. Patient, patience. Watching the weather every single day takes patience! Next time, we will walk from Harbor Town up to Hilltop Park, the island's tsunami evacuation place!

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, A typhoon brings strong wind and heavy rain. Today, Ember meets us at the harbor. He points to a green sign with an arrow. This arrow shows the way to high ground. Let's walk it together! On the way, Ember explains. A tsunami is a series of huge waves. It usually happens after an earthquake under the sea. In the deep ocean, a tsunami can travel as fast as a jet plane. So we don't wait. If you hear a warning, go to high ground. Say it with me. If you hear a warning, go to high ground. Great! We walk up a gentle slope, past little houses and a vegetable field. After about ten minutes, we reach Hilltop Park. A big camphor tree stands by the gate. Let's read the sign by the gate. "Hilltop Park, Tsunami Evacuation Place. This park is high above the sea. It takes about ten minutes to walk here from the harbor. If you hear a tsunami warning, go to high ground at once. Never go to the beach to watch the waves. More than one wave can come, so stay on high ground until the warning is over. Adults will tell you when it is safe." How long does it take to walk here from the harbor? About ten minutes. Why should you stay on high ground? Because more than one wave can come. Kiko looks down at the harbor. The sea looks so calm and blue today. Ember nods. Now we know the way, so we can feel safe. Now, phonics. Let's say nouns that end with e, n, c, y. Emergency. In an emergency, walk up to Hilltop Park. Urgent, urgency. Frequent, frequency. Fluent, fluency. Your English fluency is growing every day! Next time, we will practice listening to announcements from the island's loudspeakers!

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, If you hear a warning, go to high ground. Today, we are back in Harbor Town. On a tall pole, there is a big loudspeaker. Ember explains. In an emergency, the island uses these speakers to tell everyone what to do. After you hear an announcement, tell your family what it said. For example, The announcement said to stay inside. Say it with me. The announcement said to stay inside. Great! Now, let's practice. Ding-dong, ding-dong. A calm, clear voice comes from the speaker. Let's read the announcement. "Ding-dong. This is a drill. This is Harbor Town. A strong typhoon is coming near the island tonight. Please stay inside your house. Close your windows and curtains, and keep away from the windows. Do not go near rivers or the sea. Please listen to the radio or TV for more information. This is a drill. I'll say it again." What did the announcement say? It said to stay inside. Where should you not go? Near rivers or the sea. Haru repeats the main point. The announcement said to stay inside. Riko adds, It also said to close the windows. Ember gives everyone a thumbs-up. Good listening! If you can't hear an announcement clearly, ask an adult nearby. Ember loves his island, and he checks the speakers with the town workers every month. That's real loyalty! Now, phonics. Let's add t, y to make nouns. Safe, safety. Keep the e! Loyal, loyalty. Honest, honesty. Just add y. If you didn't hear something, say so. That's honesty. Certain, certainty. When we listen well, we know what to do with certainty. Next time, we will have a big Disaster Science Quiz at the museum!

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, The announcement said to stay inside. Today is the Disaster Science Quiz at the museum! Two teams sit behind big red buzzers. Team Lava is Haru and Kiko. Team Magma is Riko and Birimo. Dr. Mori is the quiz master, and Ember keeps the score. Dr. Mori reads the first question. What should you do during a typhoon? Say it with me. What should you do during a typhoon? Great! Beep! Kiko presses the buzzer. You should stay inside and keep away from windows. Correct! Let's read the next quiz cards. "Quiz Card Two. True or false? A tsunami is only one big wave. Quiz Card Three. What do we call melted rock under the ground? Quiz Card Four. Where do typhoons form? Quiz Card Five. During an earthquake, what should you protect first? Quiz Card Six. Why does our island have rich soil? Bonus Question. What number should you call for a fire or an ambulance in Japan?" True or false? A tsunami is only one big wave. False! More than one wave can come. What number should you call for a fire or an ambulance? One, one, nine. The answers keep coming. Magma! Over warm ocean water! Your head! Old ash from the volcano! In the end, it's a tie. Ember cheers, Everybody wins! Suddenly, the Safety Lantern glows, and the second window lights up! Now, phonics. Let's review. Assist, assistance. Thanks for your assistance, Ember! Absent, absence. Everyone came today, so there were no absences. Emergency, with e, n, c, y at the end. Safe, safety. Keep the e. Erupt, eruption. Mount Cinder's last eruption was about 300 years ago. Next time, we will pack an emergency kit together!

vocab.ja: ひじょう もちだし ぶくろ

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, What should you do during a typhoon? Today, Ember meets us at the Earth Science Museum with a big, empty backpack. He taps his yellow helmet and says, Safety first, fun always! Today, we will pack an emergency kit. An emergency kit is a bag of things you need when something big happens, like an earthquake or a typhoon. Riko asks, What goes inside? Ember smiles. The most important things come first. An emergency kit has water, food, and a flashlight. Say it with me. An emergency kit has water, food, and a flashlight. Great! Haru picks up a big bottle of water. Wow, this is heavy! Ember nods. Water is heavy, but we need a lot of it. Let's read Ember's checklist. "My Emergency Kit Checklist. Water: about three liters for each person for one day. Keep enough for at least three days. Food that keeps for a long time, like crackers and canned food. A flashlight and extra batteries. A radio, so you can hear the news. A first-aid kit for small cuts. A whistle, masks, gloves, and a warm jacket. Put copies of important papers in a waterproof bag. Check your kit often!" How much water does one person need for one day? About three liters. Why do we need a radio? So we can hear the news. Kiko packs the crackers and the canned food. Birimo tries on the gloves and waves his hands. Look, I'm ready for anything! Ember laughs. Don't forget the whistle, Birimo! Now, phonics. Proof means it keeps something out, or it's strong against something. Water plus proof is waterproof. A waterproof bag keeps the rain out. Wind plus proof is windproof. A windproof jacket keeps out the cold wind. Leak plus proof is leakproof. A leakproof bottle never drips, so your kit stays dry. Remember, we write each one as one word, with no space. Next time, we will visit a special safety house and look for the exits!

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, An emergency kit has water, food, and a flashlight. Today, Ember takes us to the Safety House at the Earth Science Museum. It looks just like a real home, with a kitchen, a bedroom, and a living room. Ember says, Let's be safety detectives! Every home has its own safety secrets. First, he points to the front door and the back door. In an emergency, you need to get out quickly. Make sure you know where the exits are. Make sure（かならず ～して ね） means do it, and check that it's done. Say it with me. Make sure you know where the exits are. Excellent! Then Haru finds a tall bookshelf in the living room. Is it safe? Ember shows us a strong strap. It fixes the shelf to the wall, so it won't fall over when the ground shakes. Let's read the card on the bedroom door. "Home Safety Check. Make sure you know where the exits are. Keep the way to the door clear of toys and boxes. Fix tall furniture to the wall. Don't put heavy things on high shelves. Put your shoes near your bed. Keep a flashlight next to your bed, and make sure the batteries work. When the ground shakes, stay away from windows and tall shelves." Where should you keep a flashlight? Next to your bed. What should you do with tall furniture? Fix it to the wall. Riko and Kiko find a big toy box in front of the back door. They move it out of the way together. Now the exit is clear! Now, phonics. Here are more proof words. Child plus proof is childproof. A childproof cap is hard for little children to open. Heat plus proof is heatproof. Put a hot pot on a heatproof mat. Shock plus proof is shockproof. My shockproof watch still works after I drop it. Next time, we will walk up to Hilltop Park and choose a family meeting place!

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, Make sure you know where the exits are. Today, we walk up the hill from Harbor Town with Ember. It takes about ten minutes. At the top is Hilltop Park, the island's tsunami evacuation place. By the gate, there's a big camphor tree. Its leaves smell fresh and sweet. Ember says, Sometimes families are in different places when something happens. Mom may be at work, and you may be at school. So every family needs a meeting place. Choose a place that is safe and easy to find. Kiko looks up at the camphor tree. Everyone on the island knows this tree! Haru says, Our family meeting place is the park. Say it with me. Our family meeting place is the park. Wonderful! Ember adds, Be clear. The park is big, so say the exact spot, like by the big camphor tree. Let's read Ember's family plan card. "Our Family Meeting Place. If we are not together when something happens, we will meet at Hilltop Park. Our exact spot is the big camphor tree by the gate. We will walk there carefully and wait for each other. If the park is not safe, we will follow the instructions of the adults there. Everyone in our family knows this plan." Where is the exact spot? By the big camphor tree at the gate. What will the family do if the park is not safe? Follow the instructions of the adults there. Birimo gives the tree a big hug. I will remember you, tree! Ember laughs. Now everyone knows where to meet. Now, phonics. Sound plus proof is soundproof. The music room has soundproof walls, so we can sing loudly. Dust plus proof is dustproof. Sand can't get inside a dustproof radio. Rust plus proof is rustproof. A rustproof ladder stays shiny, even in the rain. Next time, we will compare safety tools, like waterproof bags and fireproof boxes!

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, Our family meeting place is the park. Today, Ember takes us to the museum shop. Dr. Mori is there, too. On a long table, there are bags, boxes, and flashlights. Dr. Mori says, Let's do a test! She puts a piece of paper inside a paper bag and another piece inside a plastic bag. Then she pours water over both bags. Splash! The paper in the paper bag gets wet, but the paper in the plastic bag stays dry. Riko says, That one is waterproof! Dr. Mori nods. Keep your papers in a waterproof bag. Say it with me. Keep your papers in a waterproof bag. Perfect! Then Ember taps a small metal box. This box is fireproof. Important papers are kept in a fireproof box at home, and copies go in your emergency kit. Let's read the shop sign. "Safety Tools Corner. This waterproof bag keeps papers dry, even in heavy rain. It's very light, so it fits in any emergency kit. This fireproof box is strong and heavy. It protects important papers at home. This foolproof flashlight has only one big button, so anyone can use it, even in the dark. Which tool is best? It depends on where you use it!" Which flashlight is easy for anyone to use? The foolproof flashlight. Why is the waterproof bag good for an emergency kit? Because it's light and it keeps papers dry. Haru lifts the fireproof box. Oof! It's too heavy for my backpack! Kiko laughs. That one stays at home, Haru! Now, phonics. Fire plus proof is fireproof. Fire can't burn it. Earthquake plus proof is earthquake-proof. Look, this long word has a hyphen between earthquake and proof. The new gym at the Island School is earthquake-proof. Fool plus proof is foolproof. A foolproof tool is so easy that nobody makes a mistake. Next time, we will share our family safety plans with everyone!

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, Keep your papers in a waterproof bag. Today is Safety Plan Day at the Earth Science Museum. Ember, Dr. Mori, and many island children are sitting in the hall. Each team will share a family safety plan. Riko goes first. She holds up a big poster with a map of Harbor Town and Hilltop Park. She speaks in a clear voice. If there's an earthquake, we will go to Hilltop Park. Our meeting place is the big tree. Say it with me. If there's an earthquake, we will go to Hilltop Park. Our meeting place is the big tree. Fantastic! Next, Haru reads his team's plan. Let's read it together. "Our Family Safety Plan. Our emergency kit is by the front door. It has water, food, a flashlight, and a radio. Our papers are in a waterproof bag. If there's an earthquake, we will protect our heads and stay away from windows. When the shaking stops, we will go to Hilltop Park. Our meeting place is the big tree by the gate. In an emergency, we call 119 for a fire or an ambulance." Where is the emergency kit? By the front door. What number do you call for an ambulance? You call 119. Everybody claps. Kiko and Birimo show a drawing of their kit, with every item in a neat row. Dr. Mori smiles. These plans are clear, and they are easy to remember. Suddenly, the Safety Lantern glows. The third window lights up with a warm orange light! Ember cheers, Three windows! Safety first, fun always! Now, phonics. Let's review. Waterproof. Water plus proof. Fireproof. Fire plus proof. Emergency. Remember, it ends with e, n, c, y. Appearance. Appear plus a, n, c, e. Look at the lantern. Its appearance is brighter now! Next time, we will join an evacuation drill at the Island School!

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, If there's an earthquake, we will go to Hilltop Park. Our meeting place is the big tree. Today, we visit the Island School. The children here are very friendly, and they invite us to join their evacuation drill. A drill is practice, so nobody needs to worry. It helps our bodies remember what to do. Ember stands at the front of the classroom in his yellow helmet. He says, When the ground shakes, protect your head first. Drop down low. Cover your head. Get under a desk and hold on. Say it with me. Get under a desk and hold on. Great job! Hold on means hold the leg of the desk tightly, so the desk stays over you. Let's read the poster on the classroom wall. "When the Ground Shakes. Drop down onto your hands and knees. Get under a desk and cover your head and neck. Hold on to the desk legs until the shaking stops. Stay away from windows and tall shelves. If there is no desk, cover your head with your bag or your arms. Stay where you are until your teacher tells you to move." What do you hold on to? The desk legs. What can you use if there is no desk? Your bag or your arms. Then a bell rings. This is a drill! We all drop, cover, and hold on. All the desks are taken, so Birimo covers his head with his arms. Good thinking, Birimo! Now, phonics. Today, let's listen to lists. In a list, your voice goes up on each item and down on the last one. Drop, up. Cover, up. And hold on, down. We need water, up. Food, up. And a flashlight, down. Bring a radio, up. Batteries, up. And a whistle, down. Next time, we will practice moving out of the school slowly and quietly, with four important rules!

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, Get under a desk and hold on. Today, at the Island School, we learn what to do after the shaking stops. Ember says, Moving out of the building is like a slow parade. Slow, quiet, and in a line. If everyone hurries, people can bump into each other and fall. Haru asks, So what's the secret? Ember smiles. Stay calm. Follow your teacher. Say it with me. Stay calm. Follow your teacher. Wonderful! Then Ember writes four rules on the board. Schools in Japan have a special word for these rules, ohashimo. Let's read them. "Four Rules for Moving Out. One, don't push. Leave space between you and the person in front of you, so nobody falls. Two, don't run. Walk quickly, but carefully. Three, don't talk. Listen for your teacher's instructions. Four, don't go back. Leave your things behind, even your favorite pencil case. Never use the elevator. Use the stairs and follow your teacher." Why shouldn't we talk? Because we need to hear the teacher. What should you do with your things? Leave them behind. Kiko practices walking down the stairs slowly, holding the handrail. Birimo whispers, I'm playing a quiet turtle! Ember laughs softly. Perfect, Birimo. Slow and steady! Now, phonics. When we ask about A or B, the voice goes up on A and down on B. Is it an earthquake, up, or a typhoon, down? Should we go up, voice up, or stay here, voice down? Is the exit on the left, up, or on the right, down? When your voice goes down at the end, it means, please choose one. Next time, we will put the steps after the shaking stops in the right order!

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, Stay calm. Follow your teacher. Today, Ember gives us six cards. Each card has one step on it, but they are all mixed up! Our job is to put them in the right order. Riko reads the first card. Get under your desk. That's easy. It's the first step! Kiko picks up the next card. Wait until the shaking stops. Then Haru asks, And after that? Can we go out right away? Ember says, As soon as the shaking stops, go outside carefully. Say it with me. As soon as the shaking stops, go outside carefully. Super! As soon as means right after something happens. But remember, carefully means we listen to the teacher and walk with our class. Let's read the cards in order. "After the Shaking. First, get under your desk and hold on. Wait until the shaking stops. As soon as the shaking stops, listen to your teacher. Line up at the door and put on your helmet or hood. Then, walk down the stairs with your class. Don't use the elevator. Go to the playground and stand in your class line. Your teacher will check that everyone is there." Where do you go after the stairs? To the playground. Who checks that everyone is there? The teacher. Riko checks the order. So, first we hide, and then we wait, right? Ember nods. That's right! You're great at this! Now, phonics. More lists! Remember, up, up, and down. Stay calm, up. Listen, up. And follow your teacher, down. Check the doors, up. The windows, up. And the gas, down. This one has four items. We have rice, up. Bread, up. Crackers, up. And water, down. Next time, we will learn an important promise about going back inside the school.

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, As soon as the shaking stops, go outside carefully. Today, the Island School children are sitting on the playground after the drill. A boy says, Oh no! I left my lunch box in the classroom! Can I go back and get it? Ember shakes his head gently. Not now. After an earthquake, a building needs a safety check, even if it looks fine. Don't go back inside unless an adult says it's safe. Unless（～で なければ） means except if. Say it with me. Don't go back inside unless an adult says it's safe. Excellent! The boy nods. OK. My lunch box can wait. Let's read the Island School safety promise. "Our Safety Promise. We will stay with our class on the playground. We will not go back inside unless an adult says it's safe. We will not go near broken glass or fallen things. We will not go to the beach or the river to look around. We will listen carefully and follow the adults' instructions. Our things can wait, but our safety comes first!" Who decides when it's safe to go back inside? An adult. Which comes first, our things or our safety? Our safety. Then Riko shares a cracker from her snack bag with the boy. Here, you can have this for now! The boy smiles. Thank you! Now, phonics. Here are today's A or B questions. Do you want water, up, or juice, down? Do we use the stairs, up, or the elevator, down? That one is easy. Always use the stairs, and never use the elevator in an evacuation. Is it safe, up, or dangerous, down? Next time, we will be the hosts of a big evacuation drill at the Island School!

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, Don't go back inside unless an adult says it's safe. Today is the big evacuation drill at the Island School, and Ember has a surprise for us. You four will be the hosts! Haru and Riko will read the steps on the loudspeaker. Kiko and Birimo will help the younger children line up. Haru practices with the microphone first. First, get under your desk. As soon as the shaking stops, line up at the door. Say it with me. First, get under your desk. As soon as the shaking stops, line up at the door. Fantastic! Then Riko practices the whole announcement. Let's read it. "Good morning, everyone. This is a drill. Please listen carefully. Pretend the ground is shaking now. First, get under your desk and hold on. Stay away from the windows. As soon as the shaking stops, line up at the door. Follow your teacher down the stairs to the playground. Don't push, don't run, don't talk, and don't go back. Stay calm. You are doing great!" Where do the children go? To the playground. What are the four rules? Don't push, don't run, don't talk, and don't go back. The drill goes perfectly. All the classes walk out quietly and line up on the playground. The principal says, Wonderful hosts! Thank you! Then the Safety Lantern shines, and the fourth window lights up with a soft golden light. Four windows now! Ember does a happy little dance. Now, phonics. Let's review. Find the exits, up. The stairs, up. And the meeting place, down. Do we walk, up, or run, down? We walk, of course! Shockproof. Shock plus proof. A shockproof radio still works after you drop it. Next time, we will visit the island's volunteer center and meet a very kind, cheerful helper!

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, First, get under your desk. As soon as the shaking stops, line up at the door. Today, Ember takes us to a small wooden building near the harbor. It's the island's volunteer center. Inside, people are packing boxes and folding blankets. A cheerful older woman waves at us. Welcome, welcome! I'm Grandma Tomo. I run this center. Ember whispers, Grandma Tomo knows everybody on the island! Today, the center is getting ready for the island's Safety Festival. Haru looks at the big boxes of water bottles and asks, How can we help? Riko lifts a bottle and smiles. We can carry water. Say it with me. How can we help? We can carry water. Great! Grandma Tomo laughs. Many hands make light work! Let's read the job board on the wall. "Volunteer Jobs for Today. Carry the water bottles to the gym at the Island School. Fold the blankets and put them in the blue boxes. Check the flashlights and put in new batteries. Make name cards for the helpers. Lift heavy boxes with a partner, and bend your knees. Take a break and drink some water when you are tired. Thank you for helping our island. Helping each other makes everyone stronger." Where do the water bottles go? To the gym at the Island School. How should you lift heavy boxes? With a partner, and with your knees bent. We work all morning. Kiko and Birimo fold blankets, and Haru and Riko carry water. Then Grandma Tomo turns on an old projector and shows us photos of happy helpers. Now, phonics. Ject means throw. Pro means forward. Project. When you project a picture, you throw it forward onto a screen. A project is also a big plan. Projector. A projector is the machine that projects the pictures. Subject. Sub means under. Our subject today is helping each other! Next time, we will practice kind words for our neighbors.

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, How can we help? We can carry water. Today, Grandma Tomo takes us for a walk through Harbor Town. She says, On our island, neighbors look after each other. After strong wind or a big shake, we visit the older people and the families next door. We knock on the door and ask kind questions. Soon, we see an old man sitting on a bench with a big bag of oranges. Grandma Tomo bends down, smiles, and says, Good morning! Are you OK? Do you need anything? Say it with me. Are you OK? Do you need anything? Great! The man smiles back. I'm fine, but this bag is a little heavy. Kiko asks, Can I help you carry that? Thank you. That's very kind. Let's read Grandma Tomo's Kind Words Card. "Kind Words for Neighbors. Smile and say hello first. Speak slowly and clearly so that older people can hear you. Ask, Are you OK? Do you need anything? Then listen carefully to the answer. Always go with an adult, and never go into a house alone. If someone needs help, tell an adult right away. Small, kind words can make a big difference. A neighbor who feels lonely may feel happy all day." Why should you speak slowly and clearly? So that older people can hear you. What should you do if someone needs help? Tell an adult right away. Kiko and I carry the oranges to the man's gate. He gives each of us an orange. Thank you, kind neighbors! Now, phonics. Ject means throw. Ob means toward. Object. An object is a thing in front of you, like an orange. Objection. If you have an objection, you say, I don't agree. Interject. Inter means between. When you interject, you put a few words in while someone is talking. Excuse me, may I interject? Next time, we will go to the harbor and help travelers who don't speak Japanese.

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, Are you OK? Do you need anything? Today, we are at the harbor. A big ferry has just arrived, and many travelers are walking off the boat. Ember says, Today is the island's drill day. Soon, there will be a practice announcement. Then a calm voice comes from the speakers. This is a drill. Please go to the shelter. But the announcement is only in Japanese. A traveler with a big green backpack looks around. She doesn't understand. Riko walks up to her with a smile. Hello! Do you speak English? Yes, a little, the traveler says. It's a drill. Everyone is going to the shelter. Riko points and says, This way, please. The shelter is over there. Say it with me. This way, please. The shelter is over there. Great! Let's read the helper card from the volunteer center. "Helping Travelers. Many visitors come to our island from other countries. Some of them don't speak Japanese. Smile and say hello. Use short, easy words and speak slowly. Point and use gestures. Show the picture signs on the map. Walk with the travelers, and don't walk too fast. When you arrive, tell the staff that the travelers need help in English. Everyone should feel safe and welcome on our island." How should you speak to travelers? Slowly, with short, easy words. What should you tell the staff? That the travelers need help in English. We walk together to the shelter in the Island School gym. The traveler says, I didn't understand the announcement, but you helped me. Thank you! Now, phonics. Ject means throw. In means into. Inject. When a doctor injects medicine, the medicine goes into your body. Injection. An injection is a shot. Eject. E means out. When something is ejected, it is thrown out. A volcano can eject rocks and ash. Next time, Grandma Tomo will tell us a story about the island long ago.

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, This way, please. The shelter is over there. Today, a soft rain is falling, so we sit with Grandma Tomo in the volunteer center and drink warm tea. She opens a big picture book. This is a made-up story about our island long ago, she says. But it shows something true about helping. Fifty years ago, a big typhoon came to the island. Everyone listened to the radio and went to the shelter early, so everyone was safe. But the strong wind and big waves damaged many houses and the harbor. Then volunteers came from all over Japan. Many houses were rebuilt by volunteers. Say it with me. Many houses were rebuilt by volunteers. Great! Let's read the last page of the picture book. "After the Storm. When the wind stopped, many roofs needed fixing, and the harbor was full of mud and wood. The people felt sad, but they did not give up. Soon, ships came with volunteers from all over Japan. They brought food, tools, and warm smiles. Together, they cleaned the streets, fixed the harbor, and rebuilt many houses. Later, the people built a stronger seawall and opened a volunteer center. Now, when someone needs help, the island is ready to help back." Who came to help the island? Volunteers from all over Japan. What did the people build later? A stronger seawall and a volunteer center. Grandma Tomo closes the book and smiles. That's why I love this little center. Now, phonics. Ject means throw. Re means back. Reject. When you reject something, you throw it back and say no. Rejection. A rejection is when someone says no. Dejected. De means down. When you feel dejected, your heart feels thrown down. The people in the story felt dejected, but their new friends helped them smile again. Next time, we will act out helper role-plays together!

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, Many houses were rebuilt by volunteers. Today is Helper Role-Play Day at the volunteer center. Grandma Tomo has set up three stations. At the first station, you help a neighbor. At the second station, you guide a traveler. At the third station, you pack a bag for a cold night. Birimo loves role-play, so he puts on a big hat. I'm playing a lost traveler! I can't find the shelter! Kiko smiles and says, Don't worry. I'll show you the way. Say it with me. Don't worry. I'll show you the way. Great! Let's read the station cards. "Helper Stations. Station One: An older neighbor is sitting outside. Ask, Are you OK? Do you need anything? Station Two: A traveler is lost and doesn't speak Japanese. Say, Don't worry. I'll show you the way. Then walk together to the shelter. Station Three: Pack a bag for a cold night. Pack socks, gloves, and a warm hat. At every station, stay calm, speak kindly, and listen carefully." What do you pack at Station Three? Socks, gloves, and a warm hat. What should you do at every station? Stay calm, speak kindly, and listen carefully. Everyone finishes all three stations. Grandma Tomo claps her hands. You are real helpers now! Suddenly, Ember's Safety Lantern begins to glow. The fifth window lights up! Five windows are shining now, and only one is still dark. Now, phonics. Let's review. Project. Pro means forward, and ject means throw. Reject. Re means back, so reject means to say no. Pack socks, gloves, and a warm hat. Socks, up. Gloves, up. And a warm hat, down. Earthquake-proof. Earthquake, a hyphen, and proof. An earthquake-proof building is strong when the ground shakes. Next time, we will make safety posters for the festival!

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, Don't worry. I'll show you the way. Today, we're making posters for the island's Safety Festival. Grandma Tomo gives us big sheets of paper, colored markers, and lots of stickers. Ember says, A good poster is short, bright, and easy to understand. Riko thinks for a moment. Then she writes in big letters across the top. Be ready! Know your exits! Say it with me. Be ready! Know your exits! Great! Haru asks, What should we put on the poster? Kiko says, Let's draw an emergency kit. Birimo draws a very big salamander in a yellow helmet. That's Ember, of course! Let's read Riko's finished poster. "Be ready! Know your exits! At home and at school, find two ways out. Keep copies of important papers in a waterproof bag. We need water, food, and a flashlight. Keep about three liters of water for each person for one day, and keep enough for at least three days. If the ground shakes, drop, cover, and hold on. Stay away from windows and tall shelves. Safety first, fun always!" How many ways out should you find? Two. How much water should you keep for each person for one day? About three liters. We hang the posters on the wall of the volunteer center. Grandma Tomo says, Everyone will see these at the festival! Now, phonics. Let's review. Eruption. Rupt means burst, so an eruption is when a volcano bursts out. Safety. Safe plus t, y. Keep the e! Waterproof. Water plus proof, all in one word. We need water, food, and a flashlight. Water, up. Food, up. And a flashlight, down. Project. Pro means forward, and ject means throw. Our posters are a great project! Next time, we will read safety instructions and find out what to do first.

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, Be ready! Know your exits! Today, we're back at our little inn in Harbor Town. On the back of our room door, there's a card with a small map and some steps. Ember taps the card with his tail. When you stay in a new place, read this first! I nod and say, Read the instructions. What should you do first? Say it with me. Read the instructions. What should you do first? Great! Let's read the card together. "Evacuation Instructions. Step one: When the alarm rings, stay calm and listen to the staff. Step two: Find the arrows on the floor plan. The nearest exit is at the end of the hall. Step three: Use the stairs. Never use the elevator during an evacuation. Step four: Walk, don't run, and don't push. Step five: Go to the meeting place in front of the inn and wait for guidance from the staff." What should you do first? Stay calm and listen to the staff. Do we use the stairs or the elevator? The stairs, always. Then Birimo asks, Is the shelter near or far? Ember points at the map. The Island School gym is just a short walk away. Haru opens the door and checks the hall. Look, the exit sign is right there! Now we know the way. Now, phonics. Let's review. Interrupted. Inter means between, and rupt means break. When someone breaks in while you are talking, you are interrupted. Guidance. Guide, take away the e, and add a, n, c, e. Childproof. A childproof cap is hard for small children to open. Is the shelter near or far? Near, up. Or far, down. Injection. In means into, and ject means throw. Next time, we will write our own safety promises.

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, Read the instructions. What should you do first? Today, Grandma Tomo gives each of us a small card shaped like a star. At the top, it says, My Safety Promise. Grandma Tomo says, A promise is something small that you can do again and again. Then it becomes a good habit. Haru thinks about his emergency kit. Then he writes, I promise to check my emergency kit every month. Say it with me. I promise to check my emergency kit every month. Great! Let's read Haru's promise card. "My Safety Promise. I promise to check my emergency kit every month. On the first day of each month, I will check the water, the food, and the flashlight. I will put in new batteries if the old ones are weak. I will practice Drop, Cover, and Hold On with my family. I will remember our family meeting place. If my friends feel worried, I will say, Don't worry. We're OK. Being ready gives me confidence." When will Haru check his kit? On the first day of each month. What will Haru say if his friends feel worried? Don't worry. We're OK. Kiko promises to keep a whistle in her backpack. Riko promises to stay calm and help her little brother. Birimo promises to stay calm and help his friends! Grandma Tomo hangs our star cards on the wall. Now, phonics. Let's review. Erupt. E means out, and rupt means burst. Confidence. Confident, change the t to c, e. Fireproof. Fire plus proof, in one word. Bring a radio, batteries, and a whistle. A radio, up. Batteries, up. And a whistle, down. Object. Ob means toward, and ject means throw. A whistle is a small object, but it can be very helpful. Next time, we will go on a goodbye tour of the island.

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, I promise to check my emergency kit every month. Today is our goodbye tour of the Island of Fire. First, we visit Dr. Mori at the Volcano Watch Center. On the screens, Mount Cinder is calm, with only a little white steam. Dr. Mori says, Our cameras and sensors watch the volcano day and night. Then we walk up to Hilltop Park and sit under the big camphor tree. Ember asks, So, what did you learn on our island? Kiko stands up and says it in three sentences. When the ground shakes, get under a desk. If you hear a warning, go to high ground. Make sure your kit is ready. Say it with me. When the ground shakes, get under a desk. If you hear a warning, go to high ground. Make sure your kit is ready. Great! Let's read Dr. Mori's goodbye card. "Dear friends, thank you for visiting the Island of Fire. You learned that the earth is made of layers and that the plates move very slowly. You learned that volcanoes make hot springs, rich soil, and new islands. You practiced Drop, Cover, and Hold On, and you learned to go to high ground at a tsunami warning. Most of all, you learned to help each other. Please come back soon!" What do volcanoes make? Hot springs, rich soil, and new islands. Where should you go at a tsunami warning? To high ground. Last, we soak our feet in the island hot springs. Ember smiles. Safety first, fun always! Now, phonics. Let's review. Abruptly. When the shaking stops abruptly, it stops suddenly. Urgency. Urgent, change the t to c, y. Dustproof. A dustproof radio keeps out dust and sand. Is it a drill or a real alarm? A drill, up. Or a real alarm, down. Eject. E means out. A volcano can eject ash and rocks. Next time, it's the big Safety Festival in the island square!

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, When the ground shakes, get under a desk. If you hear a warning, go to high ground. Make sure your kit is ready. Today is the World 33 Safety Festival in the island square! Flags hang between the trees, and our posters are on every wall. Dr. Mori runs the volcano stand, and Grandma Tomo hands out warm rice balls. Then Ember climbs onto a box and holds up the Safety Lantern. He says, On this island, we learned three big things. Know it, prepare for it, and help each other. Say it with me. Know it, prepare for it, and help each other. Wonderful! Let's read the festival program. "Welcome to the World 33 Safety Festival! At the volcano stand, learn why Mount Cinder gives us hot springs. At the kit stand, pack a bag with water, food, and a flashlight. At the drill stand, practice Drop, Cover, and Hold On. At the helper stand, practice kind words in English and Japanese. Don't miss the poster corner! Thank you for keeping the Island of Fire safe and strong!" Where can you pack a bag? At the kit stand. What can you practice at the helper stand? Kind words in English and Japanese. Suddenly, the Safety Lantern shines brighter than ever. The sixth window lights up! Congratulations! All six windows are shining! A beam of light points over the hills to the small island airport. A little plane is waiting on the runway. Ember says, That plane flies to the Airport of Wings! Now, phonics. Let's review. Eruption. Rupt means burst. Emergency. Emerge, drop the last e, and add e, n, c, y. Earthquake-proof. Don't forget the hyphen. Drop, cover, and hold on. Drop, up. Cover, up. And hold on, down. Subject. Sub means under, and ject means throw. Goodbye, Ember! Goodbye, Dr. Mori and Grandma Tomo! See you at the Airport of Wings!

segments.subtitleEn: Final quiz! What's our island's message? A, Run and hide alone. B, Know it, prepare for it, and help each other. Think!

slide.title: Quiz
items: Know it, prepare for it, and help each other.

segments.say: It's B! We know, we prepare, and we help each other. You're island heroes!
segments.subtitleJa: こたえは B！ しって、そなえて、たすけあう。あなたたちは 島の ヒーローだね！
segments.subtitleEn: It's B! We know, we prepare, and we help each other. You're island heroes!

slide.title: Answer
items: Congratulations! All six windows are shining!

segments.say: What a world! You can say the big message, help visitors kindly, and stay calm and ready. Next, go and talk with Riko! After that, it's World thirty-four, the Airport of Wings! See you!
segments.subtitleJa: すばらしい ワールドだったね！ 大きな メッセージが いえて、こまって いる 人を やさしく たすけて、おちついて そなえる ことが できるよ。このあと リコちゃんと おはなし してね！ その つぎは ワールド34、つばさの空港！ バイバイ！
segments.subtitleEn: What a world! You can say the big message, help visitors kindly, and stay calm and ready. Next, go and talk with Riko! After that, it's World thirty-four, the Airport of Wings! See you!
